units.subject: Biology
units.title: Aquatic Habitat
objectives: Define aquatic habitat and distinguish freshwater from marine environments.
Explain how light, temperature, salinity, depth and dissolved oxygen affect aquatic organisms.
units.body:
Aquatic Habitat

Aquatic habitats include freshwater rivers, streams, lakes and ponds, and marine seas and oceans. Estuaries form where fresh river water mixes with seawater, so salinity changes with tides and rainfall. Light decreases with depth and limits photosynthesis; temperature affects metabolism and oxygen availability; dissolved oxygen supports aerobic respiration; salinity affects water balance. Currents, waves, pressure, turbidity and the nature of the bottom also shape the organisms that can live there. Plankton drift with water, nekton swim actively, and benthos live on or in the bottom. Phytoplankton are producers, while zooplankton commonly feed on other plankton. Habitat protection requires water-quality control, wetland protection and sustainable fishing.

Applying the concept: identify the environmental condition or biological process first, then explain how it affects an organism or ecosystem. Use a cause-and-effect sequence rather than naming terms without explanation. In a local example, state the habitat or process, identify the relevant factor, describe the biological response and explain the likely ecological consequence. Where several factors interact, avoid claiming that one factor alone caused an observed change without evidence.

Key learning check: define the main term accurately; distinguish related concepts; give a relevant example; and explain the relationship between structure, function and environment. The examples in this lesson are original teaching illustrations, not quotations from the supplied school document. The source audit records the corresponding scheme topic and body-section anchor.

units.title: Terrestrial Habitat
objectives: Define terrestrial habitat and identify major abiotic factors.

units.body:
Terrestrial Habitat

A terrestrial habitat is a land environment occupied by organisms. Climate, soil, relief and water availability influence the vegetation and animals found there. Tropical rainforests generally have high rainfall and layered vegetation. Savannas have grasses with scattered trees and often distinct wet and dry seasons. Deserts receive little rainfall, so organisms face water shortage and sometimes large daily temperature changes. Grasslands are dominated by grasses where rainfall, fire, grazing or soil conditions restrict tree cover. Rainfall, temperature, soil texture, pH, nutrients, light and wind are abiotic factors; competition, grazing, predation and mutualism are biotic factors. Organisms show features that help them function in local conditions, such as water-storing tissues, deep roots, burrowing behaviour or seasonal dormancy.

Applying the concept: identify the environmental condition or biological process first, then explain how it affects an organism or ecosystem. Use a cause-and-effect sequence rather than naming terms without explanation. In a local example, state the habitat or process, identify the relevant factor, describe the biological response and explain the likely ecological consequence. Where several factors interact, avoid claiming that one factor alone caused an observed change without evidence.

Key learning check: define the main term accurately; distinguish related concepts; give a relevant example; and explain the relationship between structure, function and environment. units.title: Food Production and Storage
objectives: Explain the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers.

units.body:
Food Production and Storage

Food production depends on ecological processes. Green plants and algae are producers: they use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into organic substances during photosynthesis. Consumers obtain energy by feeding on plants or other organisms. Decomposers, especially bacteria and fungi, break down dead material and wastes, returning nutrients to the environment. A food chain shows one feeding pathway; a food web combines connected chains. Energy is transferred between trophic levels, but some is used in life processes and dissipated as heat. Food preservation slows microorganisms and enzymes: drying removes available water, refrigeration slows microbial growth, freezing slows it further, salting and sugaring reduce water availability, and canning combines heat treatment with an airtight container. Safe storage also requires clean handling, suitable containers and pest control.

Applying the concept: identify the environmental condition or biological process first, then explain how it affects an organism or ecosystem. Use a cause-and-effect sequence rather than naming terms without explanation. In a local example, state the habitat or process, identify the relevant factor, describe the biological response and explain the likely ecological consequence. Where several factors interact, avoid claiming that one factor alone caused an observed change without evidence.

Key learning check: define the main term accurately; distinguish related concepts; give a relevant example; and explain the relationship between structure, function and environment. objectives: Explain why matter is recycled while energy flows through ecosystems.

units.body:
Nutrient Cycling in Nature

Nutrient cycling is the movement and reuse of elements between organisms and the non-living environment. Organisms need carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and other elements to build cells. Energy, in contrast, enters ecosystems mainly as sunlight and is eventually dissipated as heat. The water cycle includes evaporation from water and soil, transpiration from plants, condensation into clouds, precipitation, runoff and infiltration into the ground. Organisms also take up and return water through life processes. Carbon enters organic matter when plants and algae take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis. It passes to consumers through feeding and returns to the environment through respiration, decomposition and combustion. These cycles connect living organisms with the atmosphere, soil and water.

Use a cause-and-effect sequence rather than naming terms without explanation. In a local example, state the habitat or process, identify the relevant factor, describe the biological response and explain the likely ecological consequence. units.title: Nutrient Cycling in Nature (Continued)
objectives: Describe nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification.
Explain how fertiliser loss can affect water quality.
units.body:
Nutrient Cycling in Nature (Continued)

Nitrogen is needed to make amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids. Although atmospheric nitrogen gas is abundant, most plants cannot use it directly. Nitrogen fixation converts nitrogen gas into ammonia or related compounds and is carried out by certain microorganisms, including bacteria associated with legume root nodules. Nitrification converts ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate. Plants assimilate ammonium or nitrate into organic compounds; animals obtain nitrogen by feeding. Decomposers break down wastes and dead organisms, and ammonification releases ammonia or ammonium. Under suitable conditions, denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate to gaseous nitrogen forms that return to the atmosphere. Excess fertiliser can leach or run off into water, stimulate algal blooms and contribute to oxygen depletion when algae die and decompose.

units.body:
Pollution

Pollution is the introduction of substances or forms of energy into the environment at levels or places that cause harm. Air pollution may come from vehicle exhaust, generators, industrial emissions and open burning. Water pollution may result from sewage, oil spills, industrial discharge, fertiliser runoff and plastics. Soil pollution can follow poor waste management, excessive pesticide use and chemical leakage. Noise from traffic and machinery can interfere with communication and sleep; thermal pollution changes habitat temperature. Nutrient pollution can cause eutrophication, while pathogens in contaminated water can spread disease. Some persistent pollutants accumulate in organisms and certain substances may biomagnify through food chains. Control begins with prevention: treat sewage, manage industrial effluent, reduce waste, handle farm chemicals responsibly and prevent dumping into drains and waterways.

units.body:
Conservation of Natural Resources

Natural resources include water, soil, forests, wildlife, fish, minerals, sunlight and fossil fuels. Renewable resources can be replenished by natural processes, but may still be depleted if used faster than they recover. Non-renewable resources such as many mineral deposits and fossil fuels form over geological timescales. Conservation protects, restores and uses resources sustainably. Biodiversity includes variation within species, between species and among ecosystems. Ecosystems provide food, clean water, pollination, soil formation and nutrient cycling. In-situ conservation protects organisms in their natural habitats, for example in national parks and forest reserves. Ex-situ conservation protects them outside those habitats, for example in seed banks, botanical gardens and zoos. Reforestation, controlled harvesting, soil conservation and wetland protection support sustainable use.

units.body:
Ecological Management and Tolerance

Every organism can survive and reproduce only within a range of environmental conditions. A range of tolerance is the interval between the minimum and maximum levels of a factor that an organism can endure. Factors include temperature, salinity, pH, moisture, light, oxygen and nutrient availability. Within the range, performance is often greatest near an optimum. Conditions farther from the optimum may create stress and reduce growth, feeding or reproduction. Beyond the limits, the organism cannot survive for long. A limiting factor can restrict distribution even when other conditions are suitable. Ecological management applies this knowledge: fish ponds need suitable oxygen and temperature; riverbank vegetation can reduce erosion; soil testing and appropriate irrigation can help avoid salinity or waterlogging. Monitoring is needed because several factors may act together.

units.body:
Adaptation

An adaptation is an inherited feature that, in a particular environment, contributes to survival and reproduction. Structural adaptations are physical features, such as streamlined bodies or thick waxy leaf cuticles. Physiological adaptations are functional processes, such as producing concentrated urine to conserve water. Behavioural adaptations are activities, such as nocturnal feeding that reduces exposure to daytime heat. Populations contain inherited variation. When individuals with particular inherited variants leave more offspring in a given environment, those variants may become more common over generations through natural selection. Individuals do not acquire a useful inherited feature simply because they need it. Aquatic examples include gills and osmoregulatory mechanisms; terrestrial examples include deep roots, water-resistant coverings and burrowing behaviour. objectives: Explain the meaning and functions of tissues and the skeleton, and distinguish chitin, cartilage and bone.

units.body:
Tissue and Supporting System (Weeks 1–2)

Tissues are groups of similar cells that carry out specific functions. The skeleton is the body framework that supports the body, gives it shape and protects soft tissues and organs. The source identifies three skeletal materials in animals: chitin, cartilage and bone. Chitin is a tough, light and flexible non-living material forming the outer covering of arthropods; in some crustaceans it is strengthened by calcium carbonate and proteins. Cartilage is a connective tissue with a firm matrix and fibres; chondroblasts secrete the matrix and mature into chondrocytes in lacunae. It is flexible and acts as a shock absorber at joints. The source describes hyaline cartilage at movable joint surfaces, the trachea, bronchi and nose; white fibrous cartilage in intervertebral discs; and yellow elastic cartilage in the pinna and epiglottis. Bone contains living osteocytes, collagen fibres and mineral salts, making it rigid and strong. During development, cartilage is replaced by bone through ossification.

The three animal skeleton types are hydrostatic, exoskeleton and endoskeleton. A hydrostatic skeleton uses fluid pressure against a muscular body wall, as in earthworms and sea anemones. An exoskeleton is an external covering, commonly containing chitin, that supports and protects arthropods; growth requires shedding the old covering by moulting or ecdysis. An endoskeleton is internal, occurs in vertebrates and is made mainly of bones and cartilage. Ligaments connect bones at joints, while tendons attach muscles to bones.

The skeleton supports the body, provides its framework, protects delicate organs, enables locomotion, assists breathing through rib movement and houses bone marrow involved in blood-cell production. Vertebrate skeletons are divided into axial and appendicular parts. The axial skeleton includes the skull, ribs, sternum and vertebral column. The appendicular skeleton includes the pectoral and pelvic girdles and the fore and hind limbs. The source also includes supporting tissues in plants in this combined section; the plant subsection remains to be reconciled against the complete rendered source before this unit can be marked complete.

units.title: Mammalian Teeth
objectives: Identify the four mammalian tooth types and explain their functions.
Describe tooth structure, distinguish homodont and heterodont dentition, and interpret a dental formula.
units.body:
Mammalian Teeth (Week 3)

Mammals generally have four types of teeth: incisors, canines, premolars and molars. Incisors have flat, chisel-shaped cutting edges and are used for biting and cutting. Canines are pointed and help tear flesh or catch prey. Premolars have broad, firm surfaces for chewing, while molars grind and chew food with the premolars. Humans develop two sets of teeth: about twenty milk teeth in childhood, later replaced by up to thirty-two permanent teeth in adults. The source notes that milk dentition lacks molars, while permanent dentition includes all four tooth types.

A mammalian tooth has a crown above the gum, a root embedded in the jaw and a neck at the junction of crown and root. The pulp cavity contains blood vessels and nerves. Dentine surrounds the pulp and forms the main hard body of the tooth. Enamel covers the dentine at the crown and protects the inner tissues; it is the hardest material produced by animals. Cement covers the dentine in the root region.

Dentition describes the number, arrangement and form of teeth. Homodont dentition has teeth that are similar in shape and function and is described in the source for fishes, amphibians and reptiles. Heterodont dentition has different tooth forms with different functions and is characteristic of mammals. A dental formula expresses the numbers and kinds of teeth in the upper and lower jaws, conventionally showing one side and multiplying by two for both sides. The source provides examples for humans, dogs, cows, lions, rabbits, sheep and rats. Tooth form and arrangement are related to an animal's feeding habits.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Digestive System
objectives: Compare feeding and digestion in Hydra and Planaria.
Explain extracellular digestion and identify where it occurs in the examples studied.
Describe the digestive tract of an earthworm and explain the roles of the crop and gizzard.
Compare digestion in a bird and a human.
units.body:
Digestive System (Weeks 4–5)

Digestion breaks large food materials into small, soluble substances that can be absorbed and used by an organism. The source compares feeding and digestion in several invertebrates and vertebrates. Hydra captures small aquatic organisms with nematocysts on its tentacles. Food enters the gastrovascular cavity (enteron), where extracellular digestion occurs; cells also take up and digest food intracellularly. Planaria is a free-living flatworm with a single-opening digestive cavity. Its extendable pharynx draws in food, and its branched intestine distributes digested nutrients; undigested material leaves through the mouth. A tapeworm is parasitic and lacks an alimentary canal, absorbing already-digested nutrients from its host.

An earthworm has a complete alimentary canal: mouth, buccal cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, crop, gizzard, intestine and anus. The crop stores food temporarily. The muscular gizzard grinds food with swallowed soil particles and grit. Enzymatic digestion and absorption occur in the intestine. Indigestible soil and waste are expelled as castings; earthworm burrowing and castings help soil aeration and fertility. In a grasshopper, the foregut includes the mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, crop and gizzard; the midgut is the main site of digestion and absorption; the hindgut reabsorbs water and leads to the anus. Saliva moistens and softens food.

Birds use a beak rather than teeth. Swallowed food may be stored and softened in the crop, passes through the proventriculus, and is mechanically ground in the muscular gizzard, often with grit. Digestion and absorption are completed mainly in the small intestine. In humans, digestion involves ingestion, mechanical and chemical digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion. Teeth break food mechanically; saliva begins starch digestion. Peristalsis moves food along the oesophagus. In the stomach, churning and gastric juice begin protein digestion. In the small intestine, bile emulsifies fats and pancreatic and intestinal enzymes complete digestion; soluble products are absorbed through intestinal villi. The large intestine absorbs water and forms faeces.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Transport System
objectives: Define transport system and explain why larger organisms need specialised transport.
Compare transport in lower and higher organisms.
Identify transport materials in animals and plants and their sources/destinations.
Describe the components of blood and state their functions; distinguish blood from lymph.
units.body:
Transport System (Week 6)

A transport system moves materials from where they are produced or absorbed to where they are used, stored or removed. Organisms need transport to distribute oxygen, water, nutrients and hormones and to remove metabolic wastes. In small or unicellular organisms, diffusion and cytoplasmic streaming can move materials over short distances. Larger organisms have a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio and longer internal distances, so specialised transport systems are required.

Materials transported in animals include oxygen from respiratory surfaces to cells, carbon dioxide from cells to respiratory surfaces, digested nutrients from the small intestine to tissues, hormones from endocrine glands to target organs, and wastes to excretory organs. Plants transport water and mineral salts from roots, manufactured food from leaves, and other substances such as amino acids and hormones. Transport media described in the source include cytoplasm, cell sap/latex, blood and lymph. Hydra distributes materials through its gastrovascular cavity; flatworms rely on a branched gut and diffusion; insects and many molluscs have an open circulatory system in which circulating fluid enters body spaces (haemocoels).

In mammals, blood and lymph are the transport media. Blood consists of plasma and formed elements: red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Red blood cells contain haemoglobin and transport oxygen. White blood cells defend the body through phagocytosis and antibody production. Platelets help blood clot. Plasma is mainly water and carries dissolved nutrients, hormones, wastes, proteins and salts. Lymph is a tissue fluid-derived liquid that contains lymphocytes and normally lacks red blood cells; it contributes to defence and transports absorbed fats from intestinal lacteals. Blood transports gases, nutrients, wastes and hormones, distributes heat, supports defence and enables clotting.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Circulatory System
objectives: Describe the protective functions of blood and outline clot formation.
Distinguish open and closed circulatory systems and single and double circulation.
Compare arteries, veins and capillaries.
Describe the chambers, valves and pumping phases of the human heart.
units.body:
Circulatory System (Week 7)

Blood has transport and protective functions. White blood cells contribute to defence through phagocytosis and antibody production; antibodies bind specific antigens, while antitoxins neutralise toxins. Vaccination exposes the immune system to a safe form or component of an antigen so that protection can develop. Platelets and clotting proteins help limit blood loss and reduce the entry of pathogens through a wound. The source describes clot formation as a sequence involving platelet activity, conversion of prothrombin to thrombin, and conversion of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh that traps blood cells.

Circulatory systems may be open or closed. In an open system, circulating fluid leaves vessels and bathes tissues in body spaces called haemocoels; this occurs in arthropods and some molluscs. In a closed system, blood remains within vessels, as in annelids and vertebrates. Fish have single circulation: blood passes through the heart once during a complete circuit. Mammals have double circulation: blood passes through the heart twice in a complete circuit, through pulmonary and systemic pathways.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return blood to the heart. Arterioles lead towards capillaries, and venules carry blood from capillaries towards veins. Capillary walls are thin, allowing exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes. Pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein are exceptions to the usual oxygenation pattern. The mammalian heart is a muscular organ enclosed by the pericardium. The human heart has four chambers: right and left atria (auricles) and right and left ventricles, separated by a septum. Valves help maintain one-way flow. The right side pumps blood to the lungs; the left side pumps blood to the body. The cardiac cycle includes relaxation (diastole) and contraction (systole).

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Transport in Higher Plants
objectives: Explain why plants require transport systems.
Distinguish the functions of xylem and phloem.
Describe water uptake by roots and the movement of water through xylem.
Explain transpiration pull and translocation from sources to sinks.
units.body:
Transport in Higher Plants (Week 8)

Plants must move water and dissolved mineral salts from the roots to stems and leaves, and distribute manufactured food from photosynthetic tissues to growing and storage regions. Water enters root hair cells from the soil by osmosis, moving down a water-potential gradient across a selectively permeable membrane. Mineral ions are absorbed by root cells, often by active transport. Water and dissolved minerals move through the xylem; manufactured sugars and other organic solutes move through the phloem.

The xylem is made of specialised conducting elements and also provides mechanical support. Water movement through xylem is driven mainly by transpiration pull: evaporation from leaf surfaces lowers water potential in the leaf and creates tension that pulls a continuous column of water upwards. Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls help maintain the column. Root pressure may contribute under some conditions but is not the main force in tall plants. Transpiration is the loss of water vapour, chiefly through stomata; its rate is influenced by light, temperature, humidity, wind and water availability.

Phloem translocates sugars, commonly sucrose, from sources such as mature leaves to sinks such as roots, fruits, seeds and growing tissues. Translocation can occur in different directions in different sieve tubes according to source-sink relationships. Xylem transport is predominantly upward from roots, whereas phloem translocation distributes organic products between sources and sinks.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Respiratory System
objectives: Compare respiratory structures and gas exchange in fish, insects and toads.
Trace the pathway of air through the human respiratory system.
Explain inhalation and exhalation in mammals.
Distinguish external respiration from cellular respiration and compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
Describe gaseous exchange in plants through stomata and lenticels.
units.body:
Respiratory System (Weeks 9–10)

Respiration includes gas exchange and the cellular reactions that release energy from food. Respiratory surfaces are effective when they are thin, moist and have a large surface area with an adequate blood supply or other transport mechanism. The source compares respiratory structures in organisms including insects, fish and toads. Insects use a tracheal system: air enters through spiracles and passes through tracheae and finer tracheoles close to tissues. Fish exchange gases across gill surfaces as water passes over the gill filaments and lamellae. Toads can exchange gases through moist skin (cutaneous respiration), the buccal cavity and lungs; the relative contribution depends on the environment and activity.

Mammalian lungs lie in the thorax. Air passes through the nose or mouth, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to alveoli. The epiglottis helps prevent food entering the airway. Cartilage supports the trachea and bronchi. Alveoli provide a large, thin, moist surface closely associated with blood capillaries for diffusion. During inhalation, external intercostal muscles contract, ribs move upward and outward, and the diaphragm contracts and flattens. Thoracic volume increases and air enters. During quiet exhalation, these muscles relax, ribs move down and inward, the diaphragm becomes dome-shaped, thoracic volume decreases and air leaves.

External respiration refers to breathing and gas exchange between respiratory surfaces and blood; internal/cellular respiration refers to energy-releasing chemical reactions in cells. Glycolysis begins glucose breakdown in the cytoplasm. In aerobic respiration, further oxidation uses oxygen and yields carbon dioxide, water and ATP; anaerobic pathways release less ATP and may produce lactic acid in animals or ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast and some plant tissues. Plants exchange gases by diffusion through stomata and lenticels; guard cells regulate stomatal opening and closing.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Excretion in Lower Organisms
objectives: Define excretion and distinguish it from egestion.
Identify excretory structures in representative organisms.
Explain the operation of contractile vacuoles, flame cells, nephridia and Malpighian tubules.
units.body:
Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products from an organism. It differs from egestion, which removes undigested food as faeces. Excretion prevents harmful waste accumulation and helps maintain internal water and salt balance. The source compares excretory structures: contractile vacuoles in protozoa, flame cells in flatworms, nephridia in earthworms, green glands in crustaceans, Malpighian tubules in insects, and kidneys in vertebrates. Plants remove or store wastes through structures and materials including stomata, lenticels, leaves, gums, latex and other substances.

Freshwater protozoa are generally more concentrated than their surrounding water, so water enters by osmosis. A contractile vacuole collects excess water and periodically contracts to expel it; carbon dioxide and ammonia can diffuse across the cell membrane. In flatworms, flame cells connect to branched tubules and excretory ducts. Flagella in the flame cells help move fluid through the tubules. Earthworms have nephridia in body segments. Fluid enters through a ciliated funnel, passes along a tubule where useful salts and water can be reabsorbed, and remaining waste leaves through an excretory pore. In insects, Malpighian tubules take wastes from the haemolymph; water and useful substances are reabsorbed along the gut and rectum, leaving concentrated nitrogenous waste, largely uric acid.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Excretory System in Vertebrates and Plants
objectives: Describe the organs involved in mammalian excretion.
Label the principal regions of the kidney and parts of a nephron.
Explain ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption and tubular secretion.
Describe ways plants eliminate or store waste products.
units.body:
Mammalian excretion is carried out by several organs. The lungs remove carbon dioxide and water vapour; the skin removes water, salts and small quantities of urea in sweat; the liver processes substances and excretes bile pigments; and the kidneys remove urea, excess salts and water in urine. The urinary system includes a pair of kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra. A kidney has an outer cortex, inner medulla and renal pelvis, and contains many nephrons.

A nephron includes Bowman's capsule and glomerulus, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. Urine formation involves ultrafiltration of blood at the glomerulus, selective reabsorption of useful substances and water along the tubule, and tubular secretion of selected ions and wastes. Hormonal regulation, including antidiuretic hormone, adjusts water reabsorption and urine concentration. Kidneys also contribute to osmoregulation and acid-base balance. Plants do not have specialised kidneys; gases and water vapour leave through stomata and lenticels, while some wastes are stored in leaves, bark, fruits or other tissues and removed when these parts are shed.

units.title: Reproductive Structures and Sexual Reproduction
objectives: Identify and state functions of male and female reproductive structures.
Identify the reproductive organs of a flowering plant.

units.body:
Reproduction produces offspring and ensures continuity of a species. The source's combined Weeks 3–4 section covers male and female reproductive structures and sexual reproduction. In flowering plants, reproductive structures include stamens (anther and filament) and carpels/pistils (stigma, style and ovary containing ovules). In mammals, male structures include testes, sperm ducts, accessory glands and penis; female structures include ovaries, oviducts, uterus, cervix and vagina. The structures produce gametes, enable fertilisation and support development.

Sexual reproduction involves the formation of male and female gametes by meiosis and their fusion at fertilisation to form a diploid zygote. In humans, sperm are produced in the testes and ova in the ovaries. Fertilisation normally occurs in the oviduct; the resulting zygote divides and develops as it moves towards the uterus, where implantation and embryonic development occur. The source also discusses reproductive organs and processes; diagrams and all detailed source assessment prompts still require page-level reconciliation.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Reproduction in Plants
objectives: Label the main parts of a flower and state their reproductive functions.
Describe pollination and fertilisation in flowering plants.
Explain the changes in the ovule and ovary after fertilisation.
units.body: Flowering plants reproduce sexually through flowers. A typical flower has sepals, petals, stamens and carpels. The anther produces pollen grains containing the male gametophyte; the ovary contains ovules, each with an embryo sac and egg cell. After pollination, a pollen grain may germinate on a compatible stigma and grow a pollen tube through the style towards an ovule. The male nucleus travels down the tube and fertilisation follows. In flowering plants, double fertilisation produces a diploid zygote and a triploid endosperm nucleus. The zygote develops into an embryo; the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit. Seeds may be dispersed and germinate when suitable conditions are available.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Pollination
objectives: Define pollination and distinguish self- and cross-pollination.
Describe agents of pollination and adaptations of wind- and insect-pollinated flowers.
Differentiate pollination from fertilisation.
units.body:
Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower. It may be self-pollination, when pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant, or cross-pollination, when pollen is transferred between plants of the same species. Agents include wind, water and animals such as insects and birds.

Wind-pollinated flowers commonly produce abundant, light pollen; their anthers and stigmas may be exposed, and stigmas are often feathery to trap airborne pollen. Insect-pollinated flowers commonly attract pollinators with conspicuous petals, scent or nectar; pollen may be relatively sticky or spiny and attach to the animal. Successful pollination may be followed by pollen germination, pollen-tube growth and fertilisation. Pollination should not be confused with fertilisation: pollination transfers pollen, while fertilisation is the fusion of gamete nuclei.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Ecological Succession
objectives: Define ecological succession.
Distinguish primary and secondary succession.
Explain the roles of pioneer species and environmental change during succession.
units.body: Ecological succession is the gradual, orderly change in the species composition and structure of a community over time. It may begin on a newly exposed surface with little or no soil (primary succession) or in a previously occupied area after a disturbance where soil remains (secondary succession). Pioneer organisms colonise first and modify the environment. As soil, nutrients, shade and habitat conditions change, other communities establish and replace earlier ones. Succession may progress through a series of stages towards a relatively stable community in the prevailing conditions. The exact pathway depends on climate, substrate, disturbance and the organisms present.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Overcrowding and Food Shortage
objectives: Explain overcrowding and its effects on organisms.
Describe adaptations or processes that reduce overcrowding.
Identify causes and population effects of food shortage.
units.body:
Overcrowding occurs when the number of organisms in a habitat becomes high relative to available space and resources. It can increase competition for food, water, light, shelter and breeding sites, encourage disease transmission and lead to stress, reduced growth or reproduction, emigration and increased mortality. Organisms and populations may reduce overcrowding through territorial behaviour, pairing and spacing, swarming, emigration, dispersal of seeds and fruits, canopy formation and chemical inhibition of nearby plants.

Food shortage may result from drought, flood and other natural disasters, pests, diseases, poor storage and practices such as bush burning that reduce soil fertility or increase erosion. Scarcity of food intensifies competition; some organisms emigrate, reproduction may decline and mortality may increase. Food production and storage therefore affect the carrying capacity and stability of populations.

units.subject: Biology
units.title: Balance in Nature and Family Planning
objectives: Define population, limiting factor and environmental resistance.
Classify abiotic and biotic factors affecting population size.
Explain how interacting factors produce dynamic balance in nature.
Define family planning and identify contraception methods listed in the source.
units.body:
A population is the number of individuals of the same species living in a defined area at a particular time. Population size is influenced by abiotic factors such as temperature, water, space, light and nutrients, and biotic factors such as food, competition, natality, mortality, dispersal, parasites, predators and pathogens. A limiting factor restricts population growth. Environmental resistance is the combined effect of factors that limit population increase. The interaction of these influences may keep populations fluctuating around a dynamic balance rather than remaining fixed.

Family planning enables individuals or couples to decide the number and spacing of children. Birth-control methods described in the source include barrier methods such as condoms, hormonal methods, intrauterine devices, spermicides, sterilisation and fertility-awareness/rhythm approaches. Methods differ in effectiveness, suitability and protection against sexually transmitted infections; condoms also reduce STI transmission risk. Decisions about contraception should be made with accurate health information and appropriate clinical advice. Family planning is distinct from termination of pregnancy.
